extraction.paper_summary: This is a review paper on aluminum matrix syntactic foams (AMSFs), covering fabrication routes (pressure/counter-gravity/gas-vacuum infiltration, stir/centrifugal/buoyancy dispersion casting), macro/micro structure, densities of published foams (Table 3), and compressive mechanical properties compiled from the literature (Table 4), plus prospective automotive/aerospace applications. Reported foam densities span ~0.7-2.3 g/cm3 and compressive strengths from ~37 MPa up to ~190 MPa quasi-statically (572 MPa reported for a dynamic Al2014/cenosphere case). No new experiments are performed; all data are literature compilations.

extraction.extraction_notes: This is a review; all records are literature-compiled values from Table 4 (mechanical) cross-referenced with Table 3 (densities) by citation number. sigma_com (1% offset yield stress per ISO 13314) was mapped to strength_mpa; sigma_plt to plateau_stress_mpa; eps_den to densification_strain. '*' entries in Table 4 mean not reported and were left null. Strain rates were not given numerically ('quasi-static' vs 'dynamic' only), so strain_rate_per_s is null and the distinction is captured in specimen_notes. Densities reported as ranges in Table 3 were not assigned to specific records (left null, noted in microstructure_notes); only the single-valued density (A356/SiC, 1.81 g/cm3) was used. Particle sizes given as ranges were left null in particle_mean_diameter_um; single values (1 mm, 3 mm) were converted to µm and entered, though the paper lists them as filler sizes rather than mean diameters. Process routes were assigned only where the review's text or reference titles state them; otherwise 'other'. Counter-gravity infiltration ([5],[19]) was mapped to pressure_infiltration; microwave sintering ([61]) to powder_metallurgy. Volume/weight fractions of fillers are not reported in this review.

extraction.paper_summary: The paper studies elastomeric syntactic foams made of a Sylgard 184 PDMS matrix filled with 3M A16-500 borosilicate glass microballoons (GMB) at 10-46.2 vol%, combining cyclic uniaxial compression experiments, analytic composite theory (equivalent solid-sphere + Christensen composite spheres), and finite element homogenization of RVEs. It compares undamaged, fully debonded, and fully crushed GMB states, finding that the composite bulk modulus is drastically reduced by crushed GMBs (even 5% crushed number fraction) but nearly insensitive to debonding, while the shear modulus is reduced by both mechanisms. Debonding also produces tension-compression asymmetry and loss of major symmetry of the homogenized stiffness tensor.

extraction.paper_summary: The paper characterises Al7075-T aluminium matrix syntactic foams made by pressure infiltration casting with ceramic hollow microspheres (66 vol.%, 88 wt.%) in three size ranges (25-75, 100-250, 250-500 um), tested under quasi-static compression, Split Hopkinson Pressure Bar, ballistic impact and blast loading. Quasi-static plastic collapse stress ranged from 75-179 MPa (densities 1585-2388 kg/m3), while dynamic compressive strengths reached 203-601 MPa at strain rates of 882-1578 1/s, showing strong rate sensitivity above 1000 1/s. Concrete Damage Plasticity FE models reproduced compression, ballistic and blast responses and predicted a 20 mm thickness is needed to arrest a 7.62x39 mm projectile at 750 m/s.

extraction.paper_summary: Injection-molded PP/EPR syntactic foams with 10 vol% pores made either from Expancel PMMA microballoons (Balloon 80, Balloon 120; spherical pores) or supercritical CO2 gas foaming (Gas 50, Gas 250; elliptical pores) were tensile tested at 0.3-100 1/s and dart-impact tested at 0.1-10 m/s, and modelled with a craze-evolution constitutive law and microstructural FE. Elastic modulus was unaffected by pore shape; yield stress and strain energy dropped more for gas-foamed (elliptical) pores, and microballoon foams absorbed about 1.4x more dart-impact energy than SCF gas foams.

All quantitative mechanical results (apparent elastic modulus, yield stress, rupture strain, strain energy up to failure vs strain rate in Figs. 9-12; dart maximum load and absorbed energy in Figs. 14-15) are shown only as plots with no numeric values in text or tables, so property fields are left null; records carry composition/process/test metadata only. extraction.paper_summary: Choqueuse et al. (IFREMER, 2010) describe test methods for hollow-glass-microsphere syntactic foams used as deep-sea pipeline thermal insulation: a buoyancy-based hydrostatic compression test giving bulk modulus and crush pressure, and Iosipescu / modified Arcan shear tests. An epoxy-matrix foam (Mat A) shows near-linear hydrostatic response with crush pressure ~90 MPa versus ~50 MPa for a polyurethane-matrix foam (Mat B) with the same microspheres; Mat A shear modulus ~800 MPa; Mat B is strongly rate-sensitive and cracks at ~120% shear strain. Temperature (4-100 C) strongly affects an epoxy foam (Mat C) but no numbers are given.

extraction.extraction_notes: Text is heavily duplicated by the PDF extraction (each paragraph repeated many times); content is a 6-page conference paper with no data tables. Microsphere grade, volume fraction, densities and manufacturing route are not specified (paper only says foams are made by co-extrusion, lateral extrusion or moulding), so process_route='other' and particle details are null. Fig. 3 values (bulk modulus 2.9 GPa, crush pressure 95 MPa) are for an unnamed 'typical' material, matrix unspecified (matrix_class='other'). For hydrostatic records, modulus_mpa holds the bulk modulus and strength_mpa the crush pressure. Mat C epoxy temperature study (4, 50, 100 C) and Mat B loading-rate study are only plotted, no numbers given, so not recorded. Iosipescu shear curves (Fig. 5) and Arcan strengths (Fig. 7) not read from plots.

extraction.paper_summary: de Lorgeril, Wyss and Orbulov (Periodica Polytechnica Mech. Eng. 2011) propose a mathematical description (modified Chesler-Cram peak function plus fifth-order polynomial) of the compressive engineering stress-strain curves of pressure-infiltrated aluminium matrix syntactic foams (Al99.5, AlSi12, AlMgSi1, AlCu5, AlZn5 matrices with 64 vol% Envirospheres SL150 or SL300 ceramic microballoons). 540 upsetting tests (three aspect ratios, three heat-treatment/temperature conditions) were fitted, and only qualitative trends of compressive strength, fracture strain, structural stiffness and absorbed energy versus H/D ratio are reported in the annex tables.
extraction.extraction_notes: FLAGGED FALSE PER RULE 10 (no quantitative hollow-particle composite data), although the subject IS metal matrix syntactic foam. The paper is clearly about metal matrix syntactic foams, but it reports NO numerical property values: compressive strength, fracture strain, stiffness and absorbed energy are shown only as trend words (increase/decrease/constant/hat/valley/unknown) in Tab. 4-7 and in unreadable Figs. 4-7. Therefore no records were created. Material descriptors available for future use: matrices Al99.5, AlSi12, AlMgSi1, AlCu5, AlZn5; microballoons Envirospheres SL150 (100 um average diameter, bulk density 0.576 g/cm3 at 64 vol%) and SL300 (150 um, 0.691 g/cm3 at 64 vol%), 30-35 wt% Al2O3 / 45-50 wt% amorphous SiO2 / 19 wt% mullite / 1 wt% quartz; 64 vol% microballoons in all cases; pressure infiltration; 14 mm diameter cylinders with H/D = 1, 1.5, 2; conditions ST 20 (solution treated, 20 C), HT 20 (T6, 20 C), ST 220 (solution treated, tested at 220 C); T6 parameters in Tab. 3. The 'Density (at 64 vol%)' column in Tab. 2 refers to the microballoon bed, not the foam.

extraction.paper_summary: Kozma et al. (Int. J. Computer Theory and Engineering 2015) present a CT-image-based 'radius incrementation' circle-fitting algorithm to reconstruct the outer surfaces of ceramic hollow spheres in an aluminium matrix syntactic foam specimen (15 x 22.5 mm cylinder, 900 CT slices at 7 um resolution) and build a CAD model for finite element analysis. Only image-fitting errors (1.0-1.5 % average) are reported; no processing, density or mechanical property data of the foam are given.
extraction.extraction_notes: The material studied is an Al matrix syntactic foam with ceramic spherical shells, but the paper is purely about the image-processing/reconstruction algorithm. No composition, volume fraction, density, or mechanical/thermal property values are reported, so there are no extractable records; flagged as not a syntactic-foam data paper per rule 10 (no hollow-particle composite data).

extraction.paper_summary: Al-12Si syntactic foams were made by vacuum infiltration of a tap-packed bed (~65%) of 1-2 mm expanded soda-lime glass particles (EGP, 0.35 g/cm3) in stainless steel moulds preheated at 200-600 C. Foams had density ~1.14 g/cm3; mould preheats >=400 C caused clamping and EGP damage, lowering stiffness, 25%-strain crush strength and energy absorption but removing the yield load drop and raising energy absorption efficiency (84-88%). Liquid-nitrogen quenching of low-preheat samples produced the same effect; CTE was reduced to 17-19e-6/K for undamaged foams.

extraction.paper_summary: LM6 Al-Si alloy was vacuum-infiltrated at 700 C into packed beds (packing fraction 0.66-0.69) of 2-3 mm expanded soda-lime glass particles (EGP, 0.35 g/cc) to make syntactic metal foam beams and, in a single casting step, sandwich structures with integral Al-Si face sheets. Three-point bending gave a foam core Young's modulus of ~7007 MPa at 1.14 g/cc (power-law dependence on density, exponent ~2); FEA with this input matched sandwich stiffness within 1-3%, while the classical sandwich analytical model overestimated stiffness by 30-60% for thick faces; modelled mass savings of 11-31% versus solid Al.

extraction.paper_summary: Cheneler and Kennedy compare porous Al (salt-bead replication) with Al-Si (LM6) syntactic metal foams made by vacuum-assisted infiltration of packed beds of 2-3 mm porous expanded glass particles (EGP, 0.35 g/cc). SMFs with densities 1.00-1.19 g/cc were compression tested; stiffness, crush strength (stress at 0.25 strain) and energy absorption follow power laws in density with exponents near 3. EGP addition raises stiffness by ~2-3 GPa and crush strength by ~13 MPa relative to porous Al of equal metal fraction; FE modelling supports small reinforcement by the EGP.

extraction.paper_summary: Epoxy (E-51/100-1B) syntactic foams filled with 30 vol% 3M hollow glass microspheres (K1, S35, S60HS) were reinforced with warp-knitted spacer fabrics (B1-B4) to form 3DSMRC ternary composites, and compared with neat syntactic foam (NSF) under quasi-static compression (2 mm/min, 8 mm thick samples). Suitable WKSF (B1, B2, B4) raised yield strength by ~7-10% and compressive modulus by ~15-21% relative to NSF at nearly the same density, while NSF showed a higher peak stress; thicker-walled S60HS microspheres gave the best compression performance. A COMSOL FE model reproduced CWS60-30-B1 within ~8%.

extraction.extraction_notes: Only thermal conductivity (Table 3) and TGA data (Table 2, put in microstructure_notes) are reported numerically. Densities (Fig. 2), tensile strength/modulus (Fig. 5) and compressive strength/modulus (Fig. 6) appear only as bar charts with no numbers in text, so all mechanical fields are left null; test conditions were ISO 527 tension (2 mm/min, 100x10x4 mm) and ISO 604 compression (25 mm cubes, 2 mm/min, to 10 mm deflection). Neat resin (0 wt%) included as a baseline record. Particle density/diameter given only as ranges (0.3-0.6 g/cm3, 30-100 um) so left null. cure_or_process_temperature_c = 180 C hot-press; post-cure 10-15 h at 150 C. test_type=other denotes thermal conductivity measurement.
